Baby Dedication
BAY-bee ded-ih-KAY-shun
noun phrase
From Old English bæby (infant) + Latin dedicatio (a consecration, setting apart for a sacred purpose, from de- fully + dicare to proclaim, devote). The ceremony of baby dedication presents an infant to God before the congregation in an act of parental consecration—publicly acknowledged dependence on God’s grace for the child’s salvation—practiced by Reformed Baptist and other credobaptist churches as the alternative to infant baptism.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Baby dedication is the public presentation of a newborn or infant before the congregation of a local church, in which the parents (and the church corporately) consecrate the child to God, pray for the child’s salvation, and pledge to raise the child in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Eph. 6:4). The ceremony draws its biblical warrant from two primary sources: Hannah’s dedication of Samuel at the tabernacle (“For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition which I asked of Him”; “as long as he lives he shall be lent to the LORD”—1 Sam. 1:27–28) and the presentation of the infant Jesus at the temple (Luke 2:22–23), fulfilling the Mosaic requirement that every firstborn male be presented to the LORD (Exod. 13:2). In the Reformed Baptist tradition, baby dedication is distinguished from infant baptism by its absence of sacramental efficacy: the ceremony confers no covenant membership, no grace, and no regeneration on the infant. The parents affirm that their child is born in sin (Ps. 51:5), stands in need of regeneration by the Holy Spirit (John 3:5), and can be saved only by sovereign grace through personal faith in Christ. The congregation commits to pray for the child and to model the Christian life before them. The dedication is an act of parental faith and covenantal awareness—acknowledging that children are God’s heritage (Ps. 127:3) and that their salvation depends not on their parents’ faith but on God’s own call.

Webster 1828 Definition

Baby dedication: the public presentation of an infant to God before the congregation; an act of parental consecration and prayer, practiced in credobaptist churches as the alternative to infant baptism, carrying no sacramental efficacy but expressing faith in God’s sovereign grace over the child.

expand to see more

DEDICATION, noun. The act of setting apart or consecrating to a divine purpose or sacred use; the formal presentation of a person or thing to God, accompanied by prayer and pledge.

2. Baby dedication distinguished from infant baptism: paedobaptism administers the covenant sign to the infant on the basis of parental faith or covenant inclusion; baby dedication presents the infant to God in dependence on divine grace, withholding the sign of the covenant (baptism) until the child professes personal saving faith.

3. Biblical model: Hannah’s presentation of Samuel (1 Sam. 1:27–28)—a child prayed for, received from God, and returned to God in consecration—establishes the pattern of parental acknowledgment that the child belongs to God and must be raised for His purposes.

4. Congregational responsibility: baby dedication is not merely a private family ceremony but a public covenant in which the congregation pledges to pray for the child, model gospel truth before them, and support the parents in their discipleship vocation.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 1:27 — "For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition which I asked of Him."

1 Samuel 1:28 — "Therefore I also have lent him to the LORD; as long as he lives he shall be lent to the LORD.” So they worshiped the LORD there."

Luke 2:22 — "And when the days for their purification according to the law of Moses were completed, they brought Him up to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord —"

Modern Corruption

Baby dedication is corrupted when it is treated as a functional substitute for infant baptism, endowing the ceremony with a quasi-sacramental significance that the credobaptist theology undergirding it explicitly denies; or when it degenerates into a sentimental rite of passage disconnected from the gospel doctrine of grace.

expand to see more

In some evangelical contexts, baby dedication has absorbed the sacramental weight of paedobaptism without the theology that would ground it: parents treat the ceremony as if it secures some spiritual benefit for the child, engages the church’s covenant protection, or signals the child’s inclusion in the covenant community in a quasi-baptismal sense. This is a hybrid without scriptural warrant. If the church is credobaptist, the infant cannot be a covenant member, and the dedication ceremony cannot confer what baptism alone (following credible profession) would signify. Baby dedication rightly understood is an act of parental acknowledgment and congregational prayer—a public declaration of dependence on God’s sovereign grace, not an administration of grace itself.

A second corruption reduces baby dedication to a sentimental rite of passage—a social ceremony marking the family’s new status—with no gospel content, no instruction about the child’s sinful nature, and no explicit pledge to raise the child in the Word. This strips the ceremony of its theological substance. Hannah’s dedication of Samuel was not sentiment; it was covenant consecration growing from agonized prayer (1 Sam. 1:10–11) and genuine faith that the child belonged to God rather than to her. The parents presenting a child for dedication are affirming theological realities: the child is born in sin (Ps. 51:5), can only be saved by sovereign grace, and must be raised on the Word of God (Deut. 6:6–7)—and the congregation is pledging to support that mission.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew natan (to give, lend) and Latin dedicatio (consecration) together name the act: the child is a gift from God, and the parents’ dedication is a returning of the gift to its Giver—acknowledging God’s sovereign claim on the child’s life.

expand to see more

Latin dedicare — to consecrate, devote fully; from de- (fully) + dicare (to proclaim, set apart); the Latin root captures the act of publicly and completely setting apart the child for God’s purposes

Hebrew sha’al / sha’ul — asked, lent; Samuel’s very name means “asked of God” (1 Sam. 1:20), and Hannah’s dedication returns the asked-for child to the Asker—the theological logic of baby dedication

Latin infans — unable to speak; the infant’s voicelessness before God is precisely why parental covenant responsibility is so solemn: the parents speak for the child’s relationship to the community of faith until the child can speak for himself

Greek paraphēmi / paristanai — to present, stand alongside; Luke’s vocabulary for the temple presentation (Luke 2:22)—to bring the child and place him before the LORD in the assembly

Hebrew nahal — inheritance, heritage; Psalm 127:3 (“children are a heritage from the LORD”) provides the foundational theology: the child belongs to God first and to the parents as stewards, not owners

Usage

"The theological weight of baby dedication in the credobaptist tradition rests on the parents’ public confession: this child is born a sinner, needs to be born again, and we commit to hold before them the Word and the gospel until God’s grace produces repentance and faith."

"Baby dedication serves as an occasion for the whole congregation to renew its commitment to the next generation: to model holiness, maintain the teaching ministry that will reach the children, and pray specifically for the children of the church by name."

"Hannah’s dedication of Samuel illustrates the proper order: prayer precedes dedication (1 Sam. 1:10–11), reception of the child as God’s gift comes before consecration, and the dedication itself is an act of faith that the child belongs to God not as a magical protection but as a theological conviction."
